methodIntro: From the papers found to a direction with a verifiable rationale.

methodSections.definition: Which direction can become a trend
methodSections.brief: Where the direction description comes from

methodGuide.definition: The radar looks for new technologies that are appearing at once in research papers, trade media and company sites, patents and adoption events. One popular paper or one press release is not enough: it needs independent confirmation, a link to your query and a description confirmed by quotes.
methodGuide.counts: Repeated versions of one scientific paper count as one paper. Repositories, releases and other sources are shown separately: they cannot be added to papers. The number of GitHub stars does not determine the ranking position.
methodGuide.history: The share of the direction's papers is compared between the recent and the previous period. This way growth of the whole collected corpus is not passed off as growth of one direction. If period coverage is unknown, the comparison is unavailable; a gap on the chart does not mean zero.
methodGuide.earliest: This is the earliest dated paper found in the examined set. It does not prove that the technology appeared exactly then. An incomplete date stays incomplete: a year is not turned into an invented day.
methodGuide.brief: Each direction needs three confirmations: which problem the approach solves, which advantage the authors claim and which example they studied. Source excerpts are attached to the claims. A laboratory result by itself does not prove industrial use.
methodGuide.order: First a candidate must pass the relevance, date and description completeness checks. Confirmed weak signals — a model decision plus a second independent source — come first, then the rest by model score and rules. If fewer than 15 technologies pass every check, the list is filled up to fifteen with the best of those that did not; each of them carries a badge naming the check it missed. Mature technologies, standards, hype, noise and off-topic items are never added.
methodGuide.limitations: The result depends on the available sources and the chosen period. An empty ranking means that this analysis lacked confirmations, not that the field has no promising ideas. Exact periods, thresholds and rules are available in the method of every saved analysis.

demo.previewIntro: The RAG preset uses sources available to you and the regular analysis pipeline.
demo.summary: Short queries often lack context. HyDE and Query2doc use generated text to help retrieve relevant real documents.
demo.title: Example: retrieval through generated documents
demo.provenance: Two scientific papers: HyDE and Query2doc · 2022–2023
demo.status: A teaching walkthrough prepared manually from the papers. It is an example of reading a direction, not a result of automatic trend selection.
demo.problem: How can a search system find relevant documents when a query is short, ambiguous or has no labelled examples? Both studies use a language model to add context before retrieval.

query.title: Ask a question
query.body: A user writes an ordinary search query.

document.title: Add context
document.body: A model generates a hypothetical document or text that expands the query.

retrieval.title: Find sources
retrieval.body: The search system uses this context to retrieve real documents.

demo.hyde: HyDE embeds a hypothetical document and retrieves nearby real documents from the corpus. The authors study retrieval without relevance labels and report improvements over Contriever. They explicitly note that the generated document may contain incorrect details.
demo.query2doc: Query2doc expands a query with generated pseudo-documents. The authors report a 3–15% improvement for BM25 on information-retrieval datasets including MS MARCO and TREC DL, without model fine-tuning. This describes specific experiments, not a promise of the same gain in your system.
demo.limitTitle: Why this does not yet establish a trend
demo.limit: Two papers show the idea and research results. A conclusion about the direction's growth needs comparable data across periods and a broader set of papers. This example has no computed rank or dynamics; it also does not confirm industrial adoption of the technology.
demo.next: One next step is to compare your existing search with query expansion using real queries from your team. Check whether relevant documents are retrieved more often, and measure latency and cost. Treat generated text as a retrieval aid; ground answers in the actual sources found.

2024_acl-long_115.name: REANO · connecting passages
2024_acl-long_115.body: Knowledge graph generation helps the reader model account for dependencies between retrieved passages.

2025_findings-naacl_232.name: GRAG · subgraph retrieval
2025_findings-naacl_232.body: The context is a textual subgraph: the model uses both its content and relational structure.

2025_naacl-long_449.name: KG²RAG · expanding context
2025_naacl-long_449.body: The graph guides expansion of retrieved chunks and organizes them into coherent paragraphs.

2025_findings-acl_856.body: A graph neural network selects relevant nodes and paths, reducing large-model calls.

2025_emnlp-main_1793.body: Differentiable subgraph selection enables joint optimization of retrieval and answer generation.

explanation.graph: Conventional RAG passes retrieved passages to the model. GraphRAG also connects facts in a graph and uses those relationships to retrieve or organize context. This is a family of methods, not one technology or algorithm.
explanation.diagram: GraphRAG mechanism: documents, connected context, answer
explanation.novelty: Relational structure complements isolated-passage retrieval. This identifies a technical distinction; it does not establish worldwide priority.
explanation.coherence: After reviewing abstracts, papers merged: {{count}}. The common principle is that a graph takes part in retrieving or organising context. This is not {{count}} independent replications.
explanation.growth: Complete 2024 and 2025 windows use the same selection rule. Publications recur across {{years}} years.
explanation.impact: Authors investigate complex questions, summarization and multi-step retrieval. Their experiments do not establish usefulness on your data.
explanation.uncertainty: Independent replications and the full history of predecessors are not measured. External evidence is a curated catalogue, not a full collection. The “Emerging” stage is an analytical hypothesis based on these papers.
explanation.lexical: This group matches terms in paper titles. Counts and trajectories are reproducible; technical novelty and coherence have not received the same review as GraphRAG. Its stage therefore remains unassigned.
explanation.result: {{recent}} − {{prior}} = {{delta}} pp. This measures the direction’s changing share of corpus publications.
explanation.ratio: Share ratio: {{ratio}}×. A zero baseline has no ratio.
explanation.descriptive: This is a descriptive comparison of full years. It is not statistical proof of growth of the whole field. Paper count and share are available separately; there is no 0–100 rating.
explanation.population: All {{total}} papers of ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, EACL and Findings for 2020–2025 were reviewed in the pinned catalogue version. One title rule selected {{count}} papers: “retrieval-augmented” or a word ending in RAG. This is the search boundary, not a full list of RAG research.
explanation.dates: Dates are the months or years of the conference publication from ACL. They do not replace first preprint version dates. 2026 is excluded as incomplete. If a year's corpus has no papers, the share is undefined.
explanation.classification: GraphRAG: 39 matches for “graph” and “GRAG” were reviewed, 6 excluded — the graph was used for training, as a result or to build a test set, not as retrieved context. The labelling was done by an AI assistant from the abstracts. The other families are title-based candidates and may overlap.
explanation.safeguards: Numbers are computed on the server from actually available, ready sources with a matching hash. Re-uploading one paper does not increase the counter. With a missing or withdrawn source, coverage becomes partial and share comparison is disabled.
explanation.scienceIntro: Rotolo, Hicks and Martin’s conceptual model supplies five characteristics to examine. It frames the analysis but does not validate our classifier. Lewis and Edge explain the RAG/GraphRAG distinction. This example does not replace independent expert evaluation.
explanation.growthUnconfirmed: A growth conclusion needs available sources and comparable yearly shares. An increase in the number of papers found alone is not enough.
explanation.titles: Direction membership was checked by paper titles, not abstracts. The stage was assigned by the archive rules; a content review of each paper is still ahead.
explanation.agentic: Agentic RAG: the model plans when and what to retrieve, judges what it found and searches again. A family of approaches from multi-agent filtering to reinforcement-trained search, not one technology.
explanation.coherenceUnconfirmed: Papers selected by title terms: {{count}}. Without reviewing abstracts it cannot be claimed that they describe one principle.
explanation.coherenceTitles: Papers merged by titles: {{count}} from {{groups}} author teams. Abstracts are not reviewed yet; this is not {{count}} replications.
explanation.noveltyUnconfirmed: The first paper in the corpus is from {{year}}. A new wave of an earlier approach is possible; that is a separate question.
explanation.noveltyAgentic: Compared with a fixed query → retrieve → answer pipeline, the model decides when and what to retrieve and judges what it found. This is a difference of approach; worldwide priority is not established here.
explanation.impactAgentic: The authors study multi-step retrieval, planning and agent reliability in applied systems. Their experimental results do not prove benefit on your data.

profile.title: Signal profile
profile.hint: Six separate measurements instead of one score. Levels are screening rules of this archive, not calibrated probabilities.

novelty.label: Novelty
novelty.basis: The direction's first paper in the corpus is from {{year}}. The absence of earlier papers in the observed period does not prove world priority.

momentum.label: Momentum
momentum.basis: A percentage point measures a change in share: 2% to 3% is +1 pp. Change of the direction's share between the complete periods {{prior}} and {{recent}} under one selection rule.

coherence.label: Coherence
coherence.basis_screened: Membership checked by abstracts: the papers describe one technical principle.
coherence.basis_titles: Membership was screened by titles only. Abstracts have not been reviewed yet.
coherence.basis_unscreened: A selection by title terms. Method commonality was not checked; unrelated papers are possible.
coherence.basis_query: Membership set by an arXiv search over title and abstract. Abstracts were not reviewed; unrelated papers are possible.

spread.label: Spread
spread.basis: Author teams active in {{year}}: {{groups}}, of which new — {{fresh}}, continuing from earlier periods — {{retained}}; total teams — {{total}}. An author team is papers with shared authors; it approximates independence, not verified replications.

application.label: Applied development
application.basis: Dated repositories, releases and company sources with verifiable addresses. The catalogue is curated and incomplete; absence of evidence does not mean absence of development.
application.basisNone: No external evidence has been collected for this direction. A young direction is not cut off by this attribute.
application.basisLive: GitHub repositories found by the query and created within the period; top by stars as of the update date. The search is automatic: irrelevant repositories are possible. A repository found does not yet confirm a working or independent implementation.

concentration.label: Concentration
concentration.basis: Share of papers of the largest author team. The lower it is, the less the signal depends on one lab or one originating event.

dial.caption: The rings show how many profile signals are confirmed: the rows carry different units and share no scale. The share of screening rules passed is counted separately, in the card header.

ladder.title: Leaving the research community
ladder.hint: One idea independently picked up by another community is an earlier signal than a rising mention count.
ladder.catalog: Catalogue of external evidence: {{count}} events, all with verifiable addresses; updated {{date}}. Stars are as of the observation date, history is not reconstructed. A company statement and a confirmed result are different levels of evidence.
ladder.none: No external evidence has been collected for this direction yet. This does not mean there is none.

live.adhoc: This one-off result is not included in the overview.
live.collectingBody: Collecting papers, repositories, discussions, patents and scientific news. This page refreshes when the calculation finishes.

live.selectPeriod: Select a month on the chart to see its papers.
live.howBody: The scientific corpus is every arXiv archive: computing and AI, physics, materials, biology, mathematics, economics. A direction's field follows the categories of its papers. The map compares the last six months up to the update date with the preceding period of the same length in days. History is split into calendar months; the current month is incomplete. An author team joins papers with shared authors; circle size shows new teams in the latest period. The stage is assessed separately on completed months and the share within its field; this is a preliminary screening. Impact is the citations of the direction's papers in OpenAlex relative to the mean of its field and publication month.
live.discoveredHint: Auto-discovery groups semantically close titles and abstracts. Older updates may have used recurring title phrases. The method and sample are saved with each direction.
live.discoveredNotice: An automatically discovered direction. The method and sample composition are available in the “How this is computed” tab.

map.title: Paper dynamics
map.aria: Topic map: paper counts and increase
map.keyboardInstructions: ←/→ — directions in increasing paper count. Home/End — first/last; Enter — open.
map.basis: arXiv · compared with the previous period {{prior}}. Each circle is a topic.
map.size: A larger circle means more new author teams
map.guide: Further right means more arXiv papers over the last six months up to the update date; higher means more additional papers relative to the preceding period of the same length. Both date ranges are shown below the chart. Colour shows relative growth: 100 → 150 papers is +50%. Both scales are logarithmic: the vertical one is compressed around zero and keeps the sign, so equal vertical distances mean equal ratios rather than equal differences. GitHub, Hacker News, patents and websites complement the card.
map.groupsGuide: An author team groups papers with shared authors. A new team first appeared in this period. Size shows {{min}}–{{max}} new teams over {{period}}; a larger circle means more new teams. This is not the number of companies or individual authors.

description.by: Written by the model from the direction's papers
description.pending: The description will appear after the next collection

technologies.pending: Technologies of this direction are still being selected. Selection runs in the background after every radar collection; open the card a little later.

live.tabsLegend: A dash means the channel history was not collected; zero means the channel was collected and had no matches.
live.typesNote: Running total since the start of the period, logarithmic scale
live.typesCumulative: Each point is the total since the start of the window, not the count for that month, so the lines only rise. An uncollected month leaves a gap: it adds nothing to the total and does not reset it, but later totals are marked “≥” because they are understated.
live.typesHint: arXiv papers, new GitHub repositories, Hacker News discussions, USPTO patents and science news are shown in different colours. The current month is still incomplete. Patents and websites are a sample: “≥” means “at least this many found”, a dash means history was not collected. Patents are dated by grant, news by publication.

uniqueness.label: Own papers
uniqueness.basis: Share of the direction's papers that do not belong to other directions of this update: 100% — no shared paper, 0% — all papers belong to another direction. This is distinctness from neighbours, not world novelty of the concept.

relevance.label: Query relevance
relevance.basis: Word-based score: the share of papers found whose title contains all query words in full. Case, punctuation and hyphens do not matter; semantic closeness was not assessed separately.

impact.label: Impact
impact.basis: Citations of the direction's papers in OpenAlex relative to the mean of its field of science and publication month: 1.0× equals the field, 2.0× is twice as high. Citations for this direction have not been collected yet.
impact.basisKnown: OpenAlex as of {{date}}: {{total}} citations over {{papers}} papers; {{missing}} more papers are unknown to OpenAlex. The norm is the mean of the field of science and publication month: 1.0× equals the field, 2.0× is twice as high. Fresh papers are rarely cited yet, so young directions get this estimate later.

semantic.label: Concept distinction
semantic.missingBasis: The comparison needs papers of at least two directions and an available model. On failure the value is not replaced with zero.
semantic.basis: Comparison with {{count}} directions. Direction profile: papers — {{papers}}, sampled evenly over time. Index = 100 × (1 − closeness to the nearest direction); negative closeness counts as zero. The higher, the stronger the distinctness. The texts used and the sensitivity are in the “How this is computed” tab. Model: {{model}}, revision {{revision}}. This is not proof of world novelty.
semantic.relevanceBasis: Semantic closeness between the query and the profile of titles with available abstracts. Higher means closer in meaning. This is neither a probability nor the share of matching papers.

additional.empty: No matches in the collected sample.
additional.unavailable: Data from this source has not been received yet.

topic.emergenceMap: Keyword emergence map and keyword issue map (Yoon, 2012). For every complete month of the window each topic gets the share of papers and the share of independent author groups in the month's population, time-weighted: the last month weighs one, each earlier month 0.05 less. The mean level and the mean relative month-to-month growth are taken; the threshold is the median of the run's set of topics. A weak signal sits at or below the median level with growth above the median on both maps; a strong signal is above on both; a well-known topic is above in level without growth; everything else is latent.

modelCheck.title: Model check against the organisers’ reference set
modelCheck.intro: The radar uses a trained model to tell a weak signal from a mature technology. Here it is checked against the hundred signals from the hackathon organisers’ dataset and against technologies it never saw in training. Every number comes from the evaluation report of the same model version that runs in the radar.
modelCheck.link: How the radar model was checked against the organisers’ reference set
modelCheck.loadError: Could not load the model evaluation report.
modelCheck.about: Logistic regression, version {{version}}. The model looks at the phrase papers use for a technology in five sources: arXiv papers, the term’s history in OpenAlex, Hacker News discussions, a maturity rating by a language model and the meaning of the name itself. Each feature has its own weight, and the sum is turned into a score from 0 to 100%. A technology scoring {{threshold}}% or more is treated as a weak signal.
modelCheck.training: Training set: {{total}} technologies from five sources. The features were measured as of {{month}}, by the same code the radar uses for its candidates.

Features of each phrase are taken from five sources. All features are brought to one scale, so their weights can be compared. The table shows what share of the model’s total weight each source contributes.

modelCheck.qualityTitle: Quality on the organisers’ reference set
modelCheck.qualityIntro: The model is checked on rows it did not see in training. The reference signals and the team examples, {{rows}} technologies in total, are split into {{folds}} parts: the model is trained without one part and scores it, in turn for each part. The check is repeated {{repeats}} times with different splits. For comparison, the simplest answer “everything is a weak signal” on the same rows.
modelCheck.precisionHint: What share of the technologies the model calls weak signals really are
modelCheck.recallHint: What share of the real weak signals the model found
modelCheck.f1Hint: A combined measure of precision and recall: it is high only when both are high
modelCheck.aucHint: The probability that the model ranks a real weak signal above a technology that is not one: 50% is guessing, 100% is no mistakes
modelCheck.robustIntro: The brief requires the model to work on data it has not seen. So it was trained without a whole source or a whole area of the reference set and checked on what was left out.
modelCheck.sourceOutIntro: None of these sources’ technologies is a weak signal. The share shows how many of them the model wrongly named a signal: in the first column the source was in training and held-out rows were checked; in the second the model was trained without the whole source. Lower is better.
modelCheck.areaOutIntro: The share shows how many of an area’s signals a model that never saw this area recognised: higher is better.
modelCheck.unseenArea: Area the model did not see
modelCheck.etalonSummary: Of {{total}} reference signals, the model classifies {{weak}} as weak signals.
modelCheck.etalonHint: Each row was scored by a model that did not see that row in training, from the first repeat of the check.
modelCheck.itemsIntro: The model score runs from 0 to 100%, the threshold is about {{threshold}}%: each checking model has its own, so near the threshold the outcome may differ from the score.

file.title: Check on your own file
file.intro: Upload a table of technologies and the model scores every row the same way it scores radar candidates: by the technology's phrases in arXiv papers over 14 months, the term's history in OpenAlex, Hacker News discussions, a maturity rating by the language model and the meaning of the name. If the table is labelled, the page computes precision, recall and {{metric}}.
file.columnName: Technology name is the only required column: «Технология» (the organizers' «Технология (слабый сигнал)» also works) or {{latin}}.
file.columnLabel: Label is an optional column «класс» or «слабый сигнал» (or {{latin}}): 1, yes or weak signal means a signal; 0, no, mature, failed or noise means not a signal. An unclear label does not fail the file: the row is scored but left out of the measures.
file.columnPhrases: English phrases that papers use for the technology go in an optional column «фразы» (or {{latin}}), up to three separated by commas. Without it a language model picks the phrases, and the score depends on its choice.
file.formats: An Excel workbook as is (first sheet; title rows above the header are skipped), CSV separated by commas or semicolons, or a JSON array of objects; at most {{rows}} rows and 2 MB. Other etalon columns (companies, stage, trend, score, sources) are not used by the model and are skipped.
file.cost: A hundred rows take two to three minutes. Every phrase is a request to OpenAlex and to the language model, and the OpenAlex daily limit is shared with the radar, so check a large file in the morning and avoid repeating it without need.

modelCheck.llmRating: The maturity rating comes from the language model {{model}}: temperature 0, no reasoning, training answers collected on {{date}}. The radar asks it with the same prompt. The prompt fingerprint (SHA-256, starts with {{hash}}) is stored in the model, and the build tests fail if the prompt changes without retraining.
modelCheck.selection: The model picks its threshold and regularisation strength itself, from the training part only: that part is split into five as well, and the strictest threshold keeping recall on this inner check at {{recall}} or more — the upper end of the brief’s band — is taken. The held-out part plays no role in the choice. Thresholds of the check models range from {{low}} to {{high}}.
modelCheck.matrixTitle: Confusion matrix: reference set and team examples, average per repeat
modelCheck.abstention: Abstention. In the radar the model gives no verdict when the phrase barely occurs in the data: one arXiv paper in the window and at most one in OpenAlex, or none anywhere. By this rule the radar would defer {{signals}} of {{total}} reference signals and {{others}} rows of other sources. Here features were collected for every row in advance, so all rows are scored; without the deferred rows {{metric}} is {{f1}}.
modelCheck.slicesTitle: Slices: the number depends on what it is compared with
modelCheck.slicesIntro: The headline number uses the reference set and the team examples — mostly mature technologies that are easy to tell apart. On hard negatives — current hype — and on all rows together precision is lower. All negatives were picked by the team and there is no independent test set: this report does not guarantee the result on the organisers’ closed dataset.

all.name: All sources
all.hint: Reference set and all negatives, rows: {{rows}}; about one in six is a signal

modelCheck.ablationTitle: What the model adds to the language model’s rating
modelCheck.ablationLead: The model’s strongest feature is the maturity rating by a language model. With the same threshold rule that rating alone gives {{metric}} {{llm}}, the full model {{full}}; ranking quality is {{llmAuc}} and {{fullAuc}} respectively. The table repeats the check without each feature group in turn, five repeats.
modelCheck.ablationGain: What publication data mainly adds is fewer false signals on old, little-known technologies: the language model does not know them and takes them for new, while the term’s history in OpenAlex shows its age. The full model names the Cosmos set a signal in {{full}} of cases, the language model alone in {{llm}}; the Michael Mullany retrospective in {{fullMullany}} and {{llmMullany}}.
modelCheck.ablationWeak: The weak spot is hype the model never saw in training: the full model names it a signal in {{full}} of cases, the language model alone in {{llm}}. Publications about hype grow as fast as about a weak signal, and only the language model’s knowledge that the term is already popular tells them apart. Hype seen in training is separated better — see the source table above.
modelCheck.outageIntro: If a source does not answer, the radar substitutes the training median for its features and marks the input as unmeasured. The model is still trained with all sources — this is how it behaves on the reference set and team examples when one fails. With two sources down the radar gives no verdict.
modelCheck.aucIntro: The comparison by the measures above depends on the threshold rule: under another rule the language model rating alone can look better than the full model. Ranking quality does not depend on the threshold — it is the probability that the model ranks a reference signal above a technology from the given source: 0.5 is guessing, 1 is perfect.
